children: Iron ore futures fell on Wednesday, as rising coking coal costs continued to squeeze steel mill margins and growing port inventories underscored ample supply.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
traded 1.11% lower at 714 yuan ($106.20) a metric ton.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 1.8% lower at $97.55 a ton.
Coking coal prices are eroding steel mill profits, and continue to dominate market direction in the short-term, said analysts from Chinese broker GF Futures in a note on Wednesday.

Major coking plants announced a fourth round of coke price increases of 100-110 yuan a ton on September 1, with some mills in Hebei and Tianjin already accepting the increases, according to data from consultancy Mysteel.

Iron ore inventories at seven major ports in Australia and Brazil rose 1.33 million tons week-on-week to 14.74 million tons in the week to August 30, the second-highest level since the third quarter, Mysteel data showed.

Shipments from Australia and Brazil are entering a seasonal rebound and point to a fundamentally strong-supply and weak-demand pattern, said analysts from broker Guoyuan Futures in a note on Wednesday.
Since August, 17 Chinese steel mills have announced maintenance shutdowns, according to statistics from Mysteel.
